## Antisemitism and Jewish Politics in America

## Abstract

In the late 2010s, antisemitism re-emerged as a topic of concern in the United States

following a series of high-profile violent attacks on Jewish institutions. These concerns

intensified following the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, the ensuing war in Gaza, and

the rise of mass pro-Palestinian protests, which together sparked renewed national

debates over what constitutes antisemitism. As a result, antisemitism has now become a

central and contested issue in American political life. This dissertation examines

antisemitism and Jewish politics in the United States in the context of this

transformation.

The first chapter examines the ideological distribution of antisemitic attitudes in

America using an original survey of 3,500 Americans in 2020. We test the “horseshoe

theory” hypothesis that antisemitism is equally prevalent on the far left and the far

right. We find no evidence for this pattern, instead finding that antisemitic attitudes

appear substantially stronger on the far right, particularly among young adults. We do

find some evidence of an anti-Jewish double standard among the left, but even those

anti-Jewish attitudes among the left are smaller in magnitude3 than those on the right.

The second chapter looks at anti-Israel sentiment among Americans, particularly

among young and far left ones, using the same 3,500-person sample. We find that

younger and further left Americans do hold distinctly negative views of Israel

compared to older and/or more conservative Americans. We examine whether their

negative views are explained by an issue prioritization of the Israel/Palestine conflict or

are focused only on Israel’s government, but neither explanation appears to explain the

findings. Negative views towards Israel persist even when respondents were asked to

specifically evaluate Israel’s culture and religion.

iii


<!-- Page 6 -->


The third chapter turns to Jewish Americans themselves. Using a new sampling

methodology to survey Jewish Americans, I examine Jewish American attitudes around

antisemitism and Israel. I find that Jewish American opinion is highly divided but

consistently organized around partisan lines, with certain denominational affiliations

and the salience of Jewish identity aligning to produce distinct clusters of opinion.

Voter file analysis reveals little evidence of a large-scale partisan realignment among

Jewish Americans since October 7, despite popular narratives around Jewish Americans

becoming less Democratic. Observed polarization around attitudes thus appears to

reflect pre-existing partisan divides rather than recent political shifts.

These chapters demonstrate how antisemitism and opinions towards Israel have

become embedded within broader patterns of American political polarization. Both

antisemitic attitudes and views towards Israel in the mass public appear to be explained

by both partisan and generational divides. Among Jewish Americans, attitudes towards

Israel, antisemitism, and other Jewish topics are similarly polarized along partisan lines,

while also shaped by denominational affiliation and the salience of Jewish identity. This

dissertation shows how recent debates over antisemitism and Israel reflect and

reinforce broader divisions in American political life.

## 0 Introduction

In the late 2010s, antisemitism in America reemerged as a topic of concern. Antisemitic

incidents had begun to increase, most visibly in a series of high-profile violent attacks on

Jewish establishments. Popular discussions began to occur around the ideological roots of

antisemitism, debating whether it was stronger on the left or the right. This dissertation

began as a one-off paper in response to those events and discussions, examining the extent

and current dimensions of antisemitic attitudes in the United States.

But as antisemitism became more visible and politically salient, the scope of the project

expanded. High-profile antisemitic incidents, the rise of white nationalist rhetoric, and

the growth of anti-Israel activism pushed antisemitism further into national politics. After

the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel, the ensuing war, and the explosion of pro-

Palestinian activism in the United States, antisemitism had become not just a subject of

concern but a central and deeply polarized issue in American politics.

These developments led to the dissertation that follows, which examines antisemitism

and Jewish politics in the United States across three dimensions: the ideological distrib-

ution of antisemitic attitudes, views of Israel among young Americans and the far left,

and Jewish American attitudes towards Israel, antisemitism, and American politics.

The first chapter, Antisemitic Attitudes Across the Ideological Spectrum (coauthored with

Eitan Hersh), examines the ideological distribution of antisemitism in America in 2020.

Public accounts of antisemitism argued antisemitism in America at the time could be best

understood through “horseshoe theory,” with antisemitism being more common on both

1


<!-- Page 19 -->


the far-left and the far-right than the ideological center. We conducted an original survey

of 3500 American adults to examine both overt and more covert antisemitic attitudes

through several experiments. We included an oversample of young adults because unlike

most other forms of prejudice, antisemitism is theorized to be more common in younger

adults. We find some evidence of antisemitism on the far-left and the far-right, but overall

the data does not support horseshoe theory. Instead, we find that antisemitic attitudes

were much stronger and more common on the far right, and especially among young

adults on the far right. This chapter was published in Political Research Quarterly in 2023.

The second chapter, The Young American Left and Attitudes About Israel (co-authored

with Eitan Hersh), examines the anti-Israel attitudes of young and far-left Americans

empirically. Using the same sample as the prior chapter, we found that younger and far

left Americans have a distinctly more negative view of Israel than older and more conser-

vative Americans in 2020. We explored whether these negative views towards Israel are

driven by either a stronger issue prioritization of the Israel/Palestine conflict or a focus

on Israel’s politics and government compared to other features of the country; neither

theory seems to fully explain the negative views. Overall, we found that the young left

evaluates Israel more negatively even when it comes to culture and religion, and similarly

overall to how it sees US adversaries such as Russia and Iran. We conclude that these

age- and ideology- based cleavages around opinion towards Israel could forecast future

changes around how American foreign policy is viewed by the public and how the two

major parties – who have both been primarily supportive towards Israel – may begin

to approach the Israel/Palestine conflict going forward. This chapter was published in

Contemporary Jewry in 2022.

The third chapter, Jewish American Attitudes and Political Behavior After October 7,

examines how Jewish Americans themselves understand Israel, antisemitism, and their

intersection with American politics after October 7 and the war in Gaza. Using a new

2


<!-- Page 20 -->


methodology to survey Jewish Americans, I examine both the distribution of Jewish

American opinion and the cleavages that structure it. I find that Jewish American opinion

is highly divided but consistently organized around partisan lines, with denominational

affiliation and the salience of Jewish identity aligning with partisanship in repeated ways

to produce distinct profiles of opinion. I also find that opinions around Zionism operate

somewhat differently, functioning more like a symbolic marker of a strong Jewish identity

rather than a concrete policy view. I then look at whether these partisan divides seem to

reflect a recent realignment following October 7, with cross-pressured Jewish Democrats

moving towards the Republican Party. Using voter file data on party registration and

turnout linked to the surey data, I find little evidence of large-scale changes in partisan

affiliation, partisan identification, or voting patterns. Instead, the observed polarization

in Jewish American opinion appears to reflect pre-existing partisan divisions.

These three chapters thus trace the evolution of antisemitism and Jewish politics in the

United States over the past decade and examine their relationship to American politics.

This dissertation shows how these topics have become embedded within the broader

political polarization in America. Rather than operating as distinct or uniquely structured

issues, both antisemitic attitudes and views towards Israel appear to be filtered through

partisan identities and other aligned characteristics. Even among Jewish Americans –

who may be expected to view these issues differently – partisanship remains the strongest

predictor of opinions.

This dissertation also contributes methodologically by demonstrating the application

of a more efficient approach to surveying Jewish Americans. This sampling technique

could allow for a more detailed understanding of Jewish American political attitudes

than has historically been possible. This creates new opportunities for future research

tracking changes in Jewish American opinion over time and examining the nuances as

3


<!-- Page 21 -->


antisemitism, Israel, and related issues have become more salient in American political

debates.

Antisemitism and debates over Israel appear unlikely to diminish in importance in

the near future in American politics. Understanding how these issues are interpreted,

contested, and experienced – both by the broader American public and among Jewish

Americans specifically – will remain an important area of study. While this dissertation

identifies clear structures in public opinion correlated with partisanship, it does not

explain how individuals come to hold these views or how political developments shape

them. Future work could build on the results of this dissertation by studying the causal

pathways that link partisanship, identity, and political attitudes, as well as the frameworks

through which Americans understand and interpret issues related to antisemitism, Israel,

and Jewish identity. Continued work expanding the findings of this dissertation will be

essential for understanding not only the trajectory of antisemitism and Jewish politics

in America, but also in how identity and polarization can interact to shape American

political life more broadly.

## 1 Antisemitic Attitudes across the Ideological

## Spectrum

1.1 Introduction Antisemitism has become a growing concern in the United States. Antisemitic hate crimes

are frequent (Feinberg (2020)). Perceived concerns about the seriousness of antisemitism

are high (Smith and Schapiro (2019)). According to a 2020 poll, 62% of Americans —

and 88% of Jewish Americans — consider antisemitism a problem. Over 80% of Jewish

identifiers agreed in 2020 that antisemitism had increased over the previous five years.1

The relationship between ideology and antisemitism – whether the prejudice exists

primarily on the political left or right, or both – has long been debated.2 Recent

public-facing accounts continue to examine both the right and the left as hotspots for

antisemitism (Weiss (2019), Lipstadt (2019)).

Right-wing antisemitism in the U.S. has driven incidents like synagogue shootings in

2018 and 2019. White nationalists were seen in Charlottesville in 2017 chanting “Jews will

not replace us,” and in the 2021 siege on the Capitol they were seen with pro-Holocaust

paraphernalia.34 Violent right-wing antisemitism has also been resurgent in Europe.5

1.6 Discussion We have explored several manifestations of antisemitic attitudes, including overt antisemitic

claims as well as double standards in which Jews are held morally responsible for Israel or

must pass moral litmus tests unlike other Americans. There are many other manifestations of

antisemitism beyond what we have studied here, but they must be left to future research.

We find overt antisemitic attitudes are rare on the left but common on the right, particularly

among young adults on the right. Even when primed with information that most U.S. Jews have

favorable views toward Israel – a country disfavored by the ideological left – respondents on the

left rarely support statements such as that Jews have too much power or should be boycotted.

We find evidence on the left of anti-Jewish double standards compared to Muslim Americans

and Indian Americans. The right exhibits strong anti-Muslim double standards. However, in these

measures too, the anti-Jewish attitudes on the left are small in magnitude compared to the anti-

Jewish attitudes on the right. The right does not have an anti-Jewish double standard, but they

nevertheless attribute to Jews substantially more responsibility and culpability for Israel than the

left does. Indeed, young far-right identifiers are seven times more likely to believe that Jewish

Americans should be held to account for Israel compared to young far-left identifiers.

No one study is definitive. Future scholarship may further test the measures we have used. For

instance, one may test whether the survey responses on the right are reflective of sincerely held

prejudice or reflective of a desire to assert anti-politically correct statements. Or one may test

32


<!-- Page 50 -->


whether the left-right divide here is at least partially a reflection of less inhibition on the right in

asserting widely-held prejudicial views.

There is a large and growing body of research in political science on prejudicial attitudes.

Antisemitism has been studied much less frequently, despite research showing the lasting impact

of antisemitic stereotypes on politics including among voters who purport to reject the stereo-

types (Berinsky and Mendelberg (2005)). An important reason for political scientists to continue

to study antisemitism is that many theories of antisemitism are closely tied to political ideology.

The articulation of a “horseshoe theory” and the empirical strategy developed in this article can

help scholarship on a range of topics beyond antisemitism. For instance, this work may inform

scholarship on other forms of prejudice, such as anti-Asian prejudice, which may also have left-

wing and right-wing manifestations. The work can also shed light on mass opinion on complex

issues such as the 2022 Russia-Ukraine war, where antiwar attitudes have emerged in pockets of

the far left and far right.

Overall, the evidence in this paper suggests that antisemitic views are far more common on

the right than the left. The antisemitism that has been on prominent display in white nationalist

protests is not merely confined to a tiny group of extremists; antisemitic attitudes appear quite

common among young conservatives, and much more so than among older conservatives or

among liberals of any age.

2.6 Conclusion Young adults across the ideological spectrum have a distinctly less favorable view toward Israel

than older adults do, but the ideological young left’s critical attitudes towards Israel stand out in

particular. Compared to both older liberals and younger conservatives, as well as compared to

how they evaluate other countries that are allied with the United States, the young left’s negative

attitudes on Israel are anomalously extreme. Among very liberal 18-30 year olds, Israel is viewed

in the company of U.S. rivals such as China and Iran.

Why does the young left have these distinct attitudes? Our analysis points to negative rather

than affirmative answers to this questions. The issue-ranking exercise suggests that the young

left does not give the Israel-Palestine conflict a high priority – at least not in the time period

of our survey, in which there was relative calm between Israel and Palestine. The cultural/

political/overall analysis suggests that the young left’s negative views toward Israel are not simply

opposition to the current government of Israel. Half of the respondents on the young left view the

languages, cultures, and religions of Israel negatively, the same levels at which they view China,

Russia, and Iran.

Some of these trends are seemingly explained by polarization. For instance, President Trump

differentiated his party from Democrats through his association with Russia and his antagonism

toward Mexico. In our analysis, we see higher support on the right than the left for Russia and

lower support for Mexico – potentially a direct outcome of a polarized public following Trump’s

cues. Likewise, President Trump lent support to the Netanyahu government in Israel, which could

explain some of the higher support on the right than left for Israel.

However, polarization is likely insufficient to characterize the patterns we uncover. Younger

and older moderates hold nearly the same regard for Israel. Compared to moderates, older liberals

have slightly less support for Israel and younger conservatives have slightly more support. But

older conservatives have substantially greater support and younger liberals have substantially

less support. It is not clear why younger liberals and older conservatives would wind up much

## 3 Jewish American Attitudes

## After October 7

3.1 Introduction In the aftermath of the October 7, 2023 attacks in Israel and the ensuing war in Gaza, the

United States has simultaneously seen the growth of a large pro-Palestine activist movement

and an increase in antisemitic incidents. Debates over the relationship between antisemitism and

anti-Israel activism or anti-Zionism have often rested on claims about what Jewish Americans

think about antisemitism, Israel, and Jewish identity. But despite this heightened attention, there

remains little academic work on how Jewish Americans themselves understand the issues and

whether their opinions are unified or more deeply divided.

A key roadblock to answering these questions has been methodological. Jewish Americans

comprise a small share – around 2% – of the US population, and there is no administrative data

identifying them. As a result, survey research on Jewish Americans has historically been difficult,

time-consuming, expensive, or lacking in statistical rigor; most efforts typically involve very large

scale screening efforts or reliance on non-probability samples. Here, I use a new sampling method

based on Bayesian-Improved Surname Geocoding (BISG) applied to the national voter file, leading

to the collection of a large, probability-based sample of Jewish American registered voters at a

fraction of the normal cost.

I use the survey results to examine the structure of Jewish American public opinion on

antisemitism, Israel, and related questions in American politics. I focus specifically on whether

opinions are broadly shared across the Jewish community or divided along previously known

or theorized cleavages in the Jewish American community. I find substantial heterogeneity in

59


<!-- Page 77 -->


Jewish American opinion, with repeating patterns of division along a few demographic lines,

most prominently partisan identification, denominational affiliation, and the salience of Jewish

identity. I also find that Zionist identification seems to operate differently from the other attitudes

examined, functioning more as a symbolic marker of Jewish identity and/or institutional affiliation

rather than a consistent predictor of concrete policy preferences even around Israel.

I use the linked voter file records to examine whether this partisan divide reflects a recent

realignment among Jewish Americans. I focus on whether there is evidence of a substantial

shift of Jewish Americans towards the Republican Party, given the Republican Party’s seeming

ownership of antisemitism in the past few years. I find little evidence of widespread changes in

party registration, party identification, or voting behavior since October 7. The observed partisan

divides may thus be a reflection of pre-existing partisan cleavages rather than a new large-scale

shift in the political alignment of Jewish Americans.

All together, these findings suggest that Jewish American public opinion is both divided and

structured, but that many of these divides reflect the broader dynamics of American political

polarization at this moment rather than a unique fundamental transformation of Jewish political

behavior.

it important to care, for example.74 As a result, such measures make it difficult to interpret what

– variation in viewpoints.

This paper attempts to move beyond those limitations and more precisely characterize Jewish

American public opinion by addressing three core questions. First, what do Jewish Americans

think about Israel, antisemitism, and the new intersection between these Jewish questions and

American politics? How many identify as Zionists and anti-Zionists? What is the range and

distribution of these opinions across the Jewish community? Secondly, what cleavages structure

these opinions? Do they mirror the partisan polarization observed in the broader American public,

or do variations in Jewish identity – denomination, institutional affiliation, or identity salience –

play a more central role? Third, to the extent that partisanship structures Jewish public opinion,

does this reflect a recent political realignment due to an issue evolution around antisemitism or

is it an activation of pre-existing partisan divides?

To answer these questions, I draw on new representative survey data of Jewish American

### 3.3 Potential Cleavages in Jewish American Public Opinion Post October

7 The developments in American politics since October 7 may have increased the salience of mul-

tiple cleavages within American Jewish public opinion. Rather than assuming a single dominant

cleavage, this paper considers five different sources of heterogeneity: institutional affiliation,

denominational affiliation (particularly Orthodoxy), age, partisanship, and the salience of Jewish

identity. Each of these has been identified in prior work as a factor shaping political attitudes, and

each may plausibly structure Jewish American public opinion in the current context as well.

3.3.1 Institutional Affiliation A first potential cleavage is institutional affiliation within American Judaism. Prior work in

political science has emphasized the key role that civic and religious institutions play in shaping

individuals’ political attitudes and behavior through socialization and information (Putnam

(2000), Verba, Schlozman, and Brady (1995), Djupe and Gilbert (2009)). Individuals who are

members of and participate in such institutions are more likely to receive consistent political cues

from and adopt the dominant positions of them (Layman (2001), Leege and Kellstedt (1993)).

Although much of this work focuses on American Christianity, the same logic should apply to

American Judaism. Mainstream Jewish institutions – synagogues, federations, schools, nonprofits,

and more – tend to hold relatively unified positions on Israel and antisemitism. Affiliated Jews

may therefore be more exposed to consistent pro-Israel and anti-antisemitism messaging.

Unaffiliated Jews may lack this socialization infrastructure. They may encounter Jewish identity

largely outside of institutional contexts, seeing it instead through family, culture, and even their

personal practice rather than in communal spaces. As a result, they may form opinions about

Israel and antisemitism through more diffuse and heterogeneous pathways, leading to opinions

that are less institutionally-shaped.

The post–October 7 environment may have heightened this divide. As Israel and antisemitism

have become more politically salient and central to political discourse, institutions may have

intensified messaging and mobilization around these issues. Institutional Jews may then have

received these concentrated cues, potentially crystallizing their opinions more around these

63


<!-- Page 81 -->


reinforced shared viewpoints. Unaffiliated Jews, lacking this structured exposure, may form more

diverse opinions or conceptualize these issues differently.

If institutional affiliation is an important cleavage, unaffiliated Jews should significantly differ

from those affiliated with major denominations.

3.3.2 Orthodox Identification A second cleavage is Orthodox identity. While related to institutional affiliation, this cleavage

separates Orthodox Jews not just from unaffiliated ones but from Reform and Conservative Jews

as well.

Orthodox communities tend to be more socially and institutionally cohesive and may maintain

stronger institutional and personal ties to Israel (Heilman (2006)). Dense communal networks

and stronger communal norms may reinforced shared political attitudes. Orthodox Jews may also

experience antisemitism more frequently due to greater visible markers of Jewish identity.75

These factors may have become more salient since October 7, given the increase in antisemitic

incidents and rise in salience of antisemitism and Israel as political issues. Stronger connections to

Israel, tighter communal structures, and more direct exposure to antisemitism may lead Orthodox

Jews to have adopted more supportive views of Israel and stronger preferences for political

responses to antisemitism or anti-Zionism.

If denominational differences are primarily driven by the distinctiveness of Orthodoxy,

Orthodox Jews should differ significantly from all other denominational groups, while Reform,

Conservative, and unaffiliated Jews should appear relatively similar to each other.

3.3.3 Age and Generational Cohorts A third potential cleavage is generational. Prior work has found that younger American Jews

tend to express weaker attachment to Israel and more critical views of Israeli policy than older

cohorts (Waxman (2016), Beinart (2012)). These differences are often attributed to generational

experiences, including temporal distance from events such as the Holocaust or Israel’s founding

and early history.

The post-October 7 environment may have amplified generational differences. Younger

Jews are more likely to be on university campuses where debates over Israel, Palestine, and

antisemitism became particularly salient. As a result, they may be more exposed to competing

narratives and pro-Palestinian activist framing.

This exposure could push attitudes in different directions. Younger Jews may become more

critical of Israel and less focused on antisemitism as framed by the Republican Party if they are

sympathetic to pro-Palestinian activists. Conversely, they may exhibit a backlash effect: if they

react negatively to that activism, they may strengthen their pro-Israel attitudes and concern about

antisemitism.

If generations are an important cleavage, younger generations of Jews should hold significantly

different opinions around Israel and antisemitism than older ones.

3.3.4 Partisanship Partisanship has long been a central organizing force in American political behavior and may

structure Jewish public opinion as well. Prior work has shown how political elites and parties

help shape public opinion by taking distinct positions on issues and drawing voters’ attention to

those differences, allowing them to filter down and be adopted by mass co-partisans (Carmines

and Stimson (1989), Zaller (1992), Levendusky (2009)). As parties polarize and differentiate their

stances, mass opinion tends to follow.

Since October 7, antisemitism and Israel have increasingly become more salient in American

partisan conflict. Republican elites have emphasized these issues more strongly, while Democratic

elites have remained more tempered. These differences may have provided clear partisan cues

that now structured Jewish American opinion.

If partisanship is a significant cleavage, Jewish Republicans and Jewish Democrats should

diverge sharply in their attitudes. Jewish Republicans should be more pro-Israel, more trusting of

the Republican party, and more approving of the Republican political response to antisemitism,

while Jewish Democrats should exhibit the opposite pattern.

3.3.5 Jewish Identity Salience Finally, the strength or salience of Jewish identity may itself structure political attitudes of Jewish

Americans. Prior work shows that individuals who place greater importance on a given identity

or issue are more likely to have attitudes shaped by that identity and to align their views with

group-related concerns (Huddy (2001), Tajfel and Turner (1979)).

<!-- Page 83 -->


In the Jewish American context, Jewish individuals for whom their Jewish identity is highly

salient may place greater weight on issues relating to Israel and antisemitism. They may thus

hold more strongly developed and polarized opinions on those questions. On the other hand,

individuals with a less central Jewish identity may be less engaged with these issues and more

likely to hold weaker, less structured views.

October 7 and its aftermath may have exacerbated this cleavage by increasing the visibility

and perceived importance of Jewish-related issues. Individuals with already high levels of Jewish

identity salience may have paid closer attention, experienced these events more intensely, and

developed stronger and more defined attitudes as a result. Those with lower identity salience, by

contrast, may have been less engaged and thus less likely to form strongly held views.

If identity salience is an important cleavage, respondents with higher levels of Jewish identity

importance should hold stronger and more clearly defined opinions on questions related to Israel

and antisemitism.

3.3.6 Causality and Overlap Between Cleavages These cleavages are not mutually exclusive; many or all may be occurring at once. These cleavages

may align within individuals and reinforce one another, producing more coherent and strongly

held patterns of opinions. The cleavages may also be causally related to one another in ways or

the opinions studied in ways that preclude a straightforward causal interpretation of the results.

One example is the relationship between religiosity and partisanship, which has been the topic

of a long debate in political science. Religion could affect partisanship through a similar mecha-

nism to institutional affiliation described above – individuals’ religious beliefs and commitments

could lead them to prioritize certain political issues and/or adopt the political views they are

socialized into from their religious environments. But partisanship could also drive religion –

Margolis (2018) explores how mass partisans may adopt religious views to align with their partisan

ones. The causal relationship could also run in both directions simultaneously, with religion and

partisanship reinforcing each other over time.

Another example is the relationship between the cleavages and the attitudes studied in this

paper. The theory outlined above for an institutional cleavage assumes that institutions shape

their members’ views. But individuals could also exit institutions if they disagree with core

66


<!-- Page 84 -->


positions on Israel or antisemitism. An observed association between institutional affiliation and

opinion may thus not be caused by socialization, but instead could reflect selection in and out of

institutions.

This paper cannot resolve this debate, as the data is cross-sectional and observational in

nature. The goal is not to determine the causal mechanisms through which Jewish Americans

come to hold particular opinions, but to characterize the current structure of Jewish American

opinion broadly and identify which observable characteristics (or sets of characteristics) most

strongly differentiate groups of Jewish Americans from one another on core questions around

Israel, antisemitism, and American politics. All coefficients should thus be interpreted as condi-

tional associations – the association between each cleavage and the attitudinal outcomes after

accounting for other cleavages – rather than independent causal effects.

Despite this limitation, the descriptive approach adopted here is informative regardless of the

causal mechanisms connecting cleavages to each other and to opinions. Illuminating where the

sharpest fault lines in Jewish American political opinion lie tells us something important about the

current state of Jewish Americans and what divisions or unities have appeared since October 7.

### 3.4 Data and Methodology

3.4.1 Sampling Methodology Surveying Jewish Americans has long been a difficult problem. Jews make up only around 2%

of American adults, and no U.S. administrative data identifies households/individuals by Jewish

ethnicity or religion. These constraints have forced survey researchers interested in Jewish public

opinion into one of three flawed options: (1) conducting probability samples that yield Jewish

subsamples potentially too small for reliable analysis, (2) conducting very expensive large-scale

screening efforts across tens or hundreds of thousands of Americans to identify Jewish Americans

(like those undertaken by the Pew Research Center every few years), or (3) relying on non-proba-

bility samples drawn from organizational lists maintained by Jewish federations, synagogues, or

other institutions.

This paper uses a new methodology involving Bayesian-Improved Surname Geocoding (BISG)

for sampling Jewish Americans, developed by myself, Kyla Chasalow, Eitan Hersh, and Kosuke

Imai. BISG produces individual probabilities of group membership based on individuals’ names

67


<!-- Page 85 -->


and geographic locations. We combined three data sources – estimates of the geographic distrib-

ution of Jews in America, name frequency data from all registered voters in the United States from

the L2 national voter file, and a new dataset of Jewish obituary data – to generate a probability

of being Jewish for each individual in the voter file. These estimated probabilities were then used

to conduct stratified Poisson sampling of the voter file; individuals whose names and geographic

location suggested a higher likelihood of being Jewish had higher sampling probabilities.

Initial validation tests comparing this approach to existing survey results of Jewish Americans

suggest that our methodology successfully identified a representative cross-sample of Jewish

Americans. By dramatically improving sampling efficiency (where simple random sampling of

American adults would be expected to yield approximately 2% Jewish respondents, our BISG

approach yielded a sample of approximately 57% Jewish Americans), this approach thus allows

for random sampling of Jewish Americans in a cost-effective way that does not sacrifice statistical

rigor.76

In June 2025, we used this methodology to sample Jewish Americans from the L2 voter file. A

total of 49,546 individuals were sampled across all 50 states and DC. They were sent a postcard

inviting them to complete a brief survey on “civic, religious, and political topics.” A total of 1,765

individuals completed the survey, yielding an overall response rate of 3.6% after a single postcard

with no monetary incentive. Of those who responded, 1,004 (57%) self-identified as Jewish. The

analyses in this paper are based on these 1,004 Jewish respondents.77

The survey included a range of questions about individuals’ demographics, Jewish identity,

political opinions, and electoral behavior. The survey results were linked back to de-identified

information about party registration and election participation from the voter file. In this paper, I

analyze a series of questions about Jewish Americans’ opinions towards Israel, American politics,

antisemitism, and recent electoral behavior, looking at how structural sources of potential opinion

heterogeneity may explain variance across each domain.78

Two features of this sampling process are important to keep in mind for the analyses that follow.

First, because the sampling frame comes from the L2 voter file, the sample targets Jewish Amer-

ican registered voters, rather than all Jewish American adults. Non-registered Jewish Americans,

who may differ from registered ones, are thus not represented. Secondly, Jewish identity in this

sample is based on self-identification. Respondents were classified as Jewish only if they reported

their current religion was Judaism, or that they identified as Jewish culturally, ethnically, or in

another way without identifying as another religion. This sample thus captures both religious and

secular Jews, but excludes individuals with Jewish heritage who either claim another religious

identity or do not claim Jewish identity at all.

All analyses and estimates use survey weights derived via a two-stage weighting process.

First, inverse probability weights were derived from each respondent’s sampling probability in

the initial sampling frame. These weights were then trimmed, with the weights being capped

at the 10th percentile on the lower end and the 90th percentile on the upper end, to prevent

extreme weights from greatly affecting the variance. These weights were then raked to align with

Pew Research Center’s demographic estimates of the gender, political party, geographic region,

and age distributions of the population of Jewish Americans. Pew’s estimates are themselves

calculated from Pew’s extensive sampling of Jewish Americans and model-based estimates of the

Jewish American population. While they are thus not true population parameters, Pew’s data

is generally considered to be the best available benchmark of the Jewish American population.

Chasalow et al. (2026) shows that the estimates are stable across a variety of alternative weighting

strategies.

3.4.2 Measurement of Key Explanatory Variables The key independent variables in this paper were designed to capture distinct potential cleavages

in Jewish American public opinion: denominational affiliation, institutional affiliation, denomi-

nation, age, partisanship, and the salience of Jewish identity.

Denomination is measured using respondents’ self-reported branch of Judaism. Respondents

were able to select Reform, Conservative, Orthodox, something else, or no particular denomina-

tion. I group “something else” and “no particular denomination” into the unaffiliated category.

If denomination, particularly Orthodox Judaism, is a major cleavage, Orthodox respondents

should significantly differ from Reform, Conservative, and unaffiliated respondents, who should

otherwise appear more similar to one another.

I also use denominational affiliation with Reform, Conservative, or Orthodox Judaism as a proxy

for institutional attachment to mainstream American Jewish life. All three branches are widely

recognized streams of American Judaism, with established networks of synagogues, schools,

and other communal organizations. While other measures of engagement, such as synagogue

membership or participation in Jewish events, could captured direct forms of involvement, they

may also reflect a wide range of substantively different contexts. For example, a respondent could

belong to a small, non-traditional synagogue organized around a specific ideological orientation

(e.g., anti-Zionism) or view participation in Jewish-led activist spaces as participating in Jewish

life. Using broader measures of engagement may thus be distinct from affiliation with established

denominational institutions; I focus on the latter as a measure of institutional attachment. If

institutional attachment is a major cleavage, unaffiliated respondents should significantly differ

from all three denominational groups.

Age is measured using respondents’ birth year. Nearly all respondents self-reported this infor-

mation in the survey. For the small number who did not, I use the birth year recorded in the linked

voter file record. I group respondents into four age cohorts (ages 18-29, ages 30-49, ages 50-64,

and ages 65+) to better gauge generational changes. If age is a major cleavage, generations should

significantly differ from others.

Partisanship is measured using respondents’ self-reported party identification. I group respon-

dents into Democrats, Republicans, Independents, and other affiliations. If partisanship is a major

cleavage, respondents from different parties – particularly Democrats and Republicans – should

significantly differ from each other.

The salience of Jewish identity is measured via responses given to a question about how impor-

tant being Jewish is to their lives. Responses range from “not at all important” to “very important.”

If identity salience is a major cleavage, respondents with high levels of identity salience should

significantly differ from those with lower levels.

3.5 Jewish American Public Opinion What do Jewish Americans think about Israel, antisemitism, and the American political response

to them, and what best explains differences in their views? I turn now to survey results on five

Section 2 – denominational affiliation, Orthodox identity, generational differences, strength of

Jewish identity, and partisanship – to see which best explains variances in Jewish public opinion.

The central empirical question is not whether these cleavages exist in isolation, but which seem to

best explain the variation of Jewish public opinion, and whether the same cleavages are dominant

across questions.

Across these different questions, a consistent pattern appears: certain combinations of cleav-

ages predict opinions in similar directions, yielding three recurring predictive profiles. The first

associates Republican political identification, Orthodox denominational identification, and a high

importance of Jewish identity. The second is dominated by Democratic political identification,

sometimes with Reform or Conservative denominational identification. The third associates

operate somewhat different, predicted primarily by Jewish identity salience alone. These findings

may be expected to be cross-pressured because of their Jewish identity: models interacting parti-

3.6 Jewish American Party Registration and Voting Behavior The role of partisanship in the previous section is striking, but the results may raise a key question

about causality: do partisan divides cause a split in opinion on Jewish politics, or do splits in

opinions on Jewish politics cause a partisan divide? Do Republican Jews have stronger pro-Israel

opinions because the Republican Party has signaled those opinions, or are Jews with strong pro-

Israel views sorting into and identifying with the Republican Party?

Political parties and party elites can drive polarized opinion change if they differentiate their

stances on issues and draw voter attention to those differences, but cross-pressured voters most

attached to an identity or most passionate about an issue are more likely to switch parties when

their views conflict with their party’s position on that issue (Carsey and Layman (2006)). If that

is the case here, Jewish Americans who have the highest identity salience or who most prioritize

Israel and antisemitism may be more likely to switch parties if they feel the other party better

represents their views on those issues. Given the Republican focus on Israel and antisemitism

since October 7 along with historically high rates of Democratic identification among Jewish

Americans, this dynamic would be expected to manifest as highly engaged Jewish voters moving

from the Democratic Party towards the Republican Party.

To test whether these patterns are a reflection of partisan differentiation on Israel and Jewish

politics or an active response to it, I examine L2 voter file data linked to our survey respondents.

The L2 data records party registration, changes to registration, and turnout behavior, although

not who individuals cast votes for. Survey respondents were asked to recall their votes in the

3.7 Discussion Jewish American public opinion on Israel and antisemitism is deeply structured by partisanship.

Across all four substantive questions examined in this paper, partisan identification emerges as

the dominant predictor of opinions. While some of the characteristics examined here – such

as denominational affiliation or the salience of Jewish identity – may be causally upstream of

partisanship, the results still show that partisan identification is the strongest observable correlate

of opinion in the current moment. Even if other factors shape partisanship, partisanship itself still

seems to play a role in organizing how Jewish Americans understand and evaluate these issues.

At the same time, partisanship does not operate in isolation. Other characteristics consistently

align with different partisan identities, producing recurring and predictable patterns across

respondents. One cluster – encompassing Republican identification, Orthodox affiliation, and

high Jewish identity salience – is associated with more conservative positions. A second cluster

– comprising Democratic identification and non-Orthodox affiliation – is associated with more

liberal positions. A smaller third cluster – made up of younger, unaffiliated, and anti-Zionist

respondents – expresses distinct views that do not cleanly map onto the primary partisan divide;

their views tend to be outside the American Jewish mainstream, such as supporting a binational

111


<!-- Page 129 -->


state in Israel. These patterns suggest that Jewish American political attitudes may be structured

into aligned identity bundles, with multiple characteristics potentially reinforcing each other

rather than operating independently. Future work could build on this by using clustering or latent

class analysis to examine whether these profiles represent three latent groups of Jewish Americans

and illuminate which other Jewish issues their opinions diverge on.

Zionist identification appears to be the primary exception to this alignment pattern. It is

associated with Jewish identity salience, rather than partisanship or denomination. Zionists and

anti-Zionists also unexpectedly converge on more concrete policy outcomes: roughly half of both

groups disapprove of Netanyahu and support a two-state solution. Zionist identification is not

irrelevant to predicting these concrete opinions, but it does not predict political positions around

Israel as cleanly as one might think. Overall, Zionist identification appears to function more as a

symbolic marker of Jewish identity or institutional connection. Future work clarifying how Jewish

Americans understand Zionism and how their interpretations of it map onto identity choices and

policy preferences would help clarify the role Zionism plays in Jewish Americans’ political lives.

These findings have important implications for contemporary politics. Despite the Republican

Party’s recent prioritization of antisemitism, there is little evidence that these partisan divides

reflect a recent realignment of political behavior. Jewish Americans show minimal changes in

party registration, partisan identification, or voting patterns following October 7, suggesting that

the observed polarization in views is not driven by large-scale switching across parties. Instead,

partisan identities appear to shape how recent events are interpreted. Partisan appeals centered

on Israel or antisemitism may therefore have limited ability to sway Jewish voters across party

lines, even as these issues have become more central to partisan discourse.

These results also highlight the importance of understanding identity alignment. Denomina-

tional affiliation and Jewish identity salience do not seem to operate fully independently of

partisanship, but instead align in consistent ways to structure opinion. This pattern is consistent

with theories of social sorting and identity reinforcement (Mason (2018)), where multiple iden-

tities converge to produce more stable, coherent, and polarized worldviews. The dominance of

partisanship in this context provides further evidence of this dynamic: even respondents who

may be expected to be cross-pressured – namely Jewish Democrats with high levels of Jewish

112


<!-- Page 130 -->


identity salience – do not appear to defect from their parties broadly. Instead, partisan attachments

remain stable, suggesting that the alignment of identities may contribute to the persistence and

polarization of political attitudes.

More broadly, this paper contributes to the study of Jewish American politics by providing

new, high-quality data on a population that has historically been difficult to study. By combining

survey data with voter file records, this study offers a more comprehensive picture of Jewish

American political attitudes and behavior. The new survey methodology also provides avenues

for more frequent surveys. For example, future research could use this approach to more easily

build panel or longitudinal designs, allowing scholars to track Jewish opinion change over time

and examine the causal mechanisms behind many of the findings in this paper.

While there is little evidence of large-scale partisan realignment among Jewish Americans since

October 7, there is unfortunately little indication that Israel, antisemitism, and related issues will

recede in political importance. These topics have become increasingly central to partisan conflict

in the United States, and Jewish Americans are likely to remain deeply engaged in these debates.

Continued research on their political opinions and behavior will therefore be essential to better

understand how this community navigates an evolving political landscape in which its identity

and core concerns become increasingly central to national partisan politics.

Overt Measures

When prefaced by the prompt [with no prime], we expect support for all statements will be

highest at the ideological extremes (i.e. among very liberal identifiers and very conservative iden-

tifiers). Support for [boycott] and [power] will be particularly high for respondents identifying

studies, we also expect support for statements to be high among Black and Latino respondents.

By way of the prompt [with the prime], we seek to emphasize that American Jews are over-

whelmingly supportive of Israel (though not necessarily its political leadership). For respondents

who are more sympathetic to Palestinians than Israel, this prompt may emphasize that Jews are an

out-group with respect to that position. For respondents who are more sympathetic to Israel over

Palestinians, this prompt may emphasize that Jews are an in-group with respect to that position.

Compared to when prompted [with no prime], respondents prompted [with the prime] will

show greater support for the view that Jews are more loyal to Israel than to America. Among the

ideological left, there will be more support for the view that Jews have too much power and more

the ideological right.

If respondents have anti-Jewish sentiments only insomuch as they have anti-Israel sentiments,

then when they think about Jews holding too much power, they will think exclusively of Jewish

influence over the Israel/Palestine conflict. However, if antisemitic attitudes run deeper than the

Israel/Palestine conflict, then respondents will assert that Jews have too much power in other

domains as well, such as in government, media, and finance. We hypothesize that those on the

political extremes will be more likely to check responses beyond the Israel/Palestine conflict.

Validation check.

Are these statements perceived as antisemitic by Jews? We ask Jewish respondents if the

Double Standards.

Next, we study two experiments measuring the degree to which respondents hold US Jews to

a different standard in terms of their responsibility for the policies of the state of Israel compared

First, we compare responses to [Muslims] with responses to [Jewish]. We hypothesize that
